q: A blind tasting held in Paris in 1976, judged entirely by French palates, put Californian wines top in both the red and the white flight. What is that event now called?
exp: The name is a joke on the Greek myth in which Paris is made to award a golden apple to one of three goddesses. It stuck because a journalist happened to be in the room and reported the result abroad, and because no French panel had ever ranked New World wine above its own.

q: Old, low-yielding bush vines of two traditional varieties carried the Priorat revival of the 1980s. Which pair?
exp: Both were already planted on the old terraces, Carinena also going by Samso in Catalonia. Cabernet Sauvignon and Syrah were brought in by the incoming producers rather than inherited.

q: Spring frost is a defining hazard in Chablis. Which protection is characteristic there?
opts: Plastic tunnels closed over the rows at night
exp: Water gives up latent heat as it freezes, holding the bud near zero inside a shell of ice. Smudge pots and wind machines are also used.

opts: The vine flowers and the fertilised flowers set into berries
The vine sheds its leaves and rests until the spring
Berries colour and begin to accumulate sugar
The first leaves emerge from the buds after winter
exp: At veraison berries soften, colour and start accumulating sugar while acidity falls. It is the visual marker that ripening proper has begun.

q: A grist is built from one malt supplying almost all the fermentable extract, with small additions of darker malts for colour and flavour. What is the bulk component called?
exp: Pale ale malt and pilsner malt are the usual bases, and they carry the enzyme load that has to convert the whole mash. Speciality malts are seasoning, and a few percent will change the colour of the finished beer completely.

q: The only black grape permitted in the region's still wines gives everything from a pale rose to a barrel-aged red. Which is it?
exp: It was long made pale and served chilled, closer to a rose than a red. Warmer seasons, lower yields and barrel ageing have pushed a generation of growers toward serious reds instead.

q: Every bottle of Austrian quality wine wears a narrow red-white-red strip across the capsule. What does it certify?
opts: That the wine passed a state analysis and tasting
That the wine was bottled at the estate that grew it
That the wine is certified organic
exp: The banderole carries the national colours and pairs with the Staatliche Prufnummer printed on the label, an inspection number issued only after a laboratory analysis and a blind tasting. The controls behind it were rebuilt after the adulteration scandal of 1985 and are now among the strictest anywhere in the wine world.

q: A crossing made at Geisenheim in 1882 ripens early, yields heavily and carries low acidity, and it once covered more German vineyard than any other variety. Which?
exp: Hermann Muller crossed Riesling with what DNA analysis eventually identified as the table grape Madeleine Royale, not the Silvaner assumed for a century. It was meant to give Riesling character on lesser sites and delivered volume instead; bottled dry it is often labelled Rivaner.

q: Head north through Germany or south through New Zealand and the vineyards thin out, then stop altogether. Which limit has been reached at that edge of the belt?
opts: Not enough summer heat to ripen the fruit
Rain in quantities no vine can tolerate
Summer days that grow too long for the vine to flower properly
Ground that stays frozen right through the growing season
exp: Both belts end where the season runs out of warmth rather than where the winter turns hard: on these maritime margins the vine comes through the winter easily enough, but it cannot finish ripening in a summer that closes too early. Every advance past the old limits has come from warmer seasons, earlier varieties or a site that gathers more sun than its neighbours.

q: A house wants acidity, finesse and the capacity to age for decades. Which variety does it build that cuvee around?
exp: Chardonnay supplies the citrus and chalk line that carries a wine through very long lees ageing. Blanc de Blancs from the Cote des Blancs are often the slowest of all to open.

q: Which New York growing region is thoroughly maritime, sits east of the city, and favours Merlot and Cabernet Franc?
exp: Water on three sides gives the North Fork a long, mild autumn, and Merlot in particular struggles to ripen in the colder inland regions. Cabernet Franc is hardier and is in fact the leading red vinifera of the Finger Lakes.

q: A frost is forecast for a clear, still night in April. Which vineyard floor gives the buds the better chance?
opts: Long grass down the rows, which insulates the soil against the cold above it
Bare firmed soil, which takes in more heat by day and gives it back after dark
Freshly ploughed loose soil, which holds more air and therefore more warmth
A thick straw mulch, which reflects the heat of the ground back upward
exp: Grass and loose tilled soil both trap air, and air conducts heat poorly, so warmth stored during the day never reaches the surface at night. Growers in frost-prone regions mow the rows short and roll the ground firm ahead of a cold night for precisely that reason.
